binders: For every function p : ℝ → ℝ, corresponding to profile, and every constant c : ℝ, corresponding to speed.
Define q : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ by q(x,t)=p(x−ct); x is the spatial argument and t the temporal argument.
The first assertion quantifies over every x ∈ ℝ; the second and third independently quantify over every x,t ∈ ℝ.
In the third assertion, τ ∈ ℝ is the variable of the function being differentiated, while x is fixed and the derivative is evaluated at τ=t.
In the fourth assertion, for every x,t ∈ ℝ there exist qt,qx ∈ ℝ. These witnesses may depend on p,c,x,t; the nested existential for qx lies inside the existential for qt.

In the fifth assertion, a,b ∈ ℝ are spatial endpoints and s,t ∈ ℝ are temporal endpoints. Spatial integrability is quantified over all a,b,t, temporal flux integrability over all x,s,t, and the balance over all a,b,s,t.
The final profile-integrability condition quantifies over every a,b ∈ ℝ. The flux function is F(z)=cz for real state z.
hypotheses: There are no additional hypotheses on p or c. Differentiability and interval integrability appear as sides of equivalences, not as assumptions of the whole proposition.
All scalar and value structures are the supplied real field, real normed-space structure and real metric topology. Integration uses μ, the distinguished measure extracted from Real.measureSpace.
conclusions: For every x,t ∈ ℝ, the real function τ ↦ q(x+cτ,τ) has derivative 0 at τ=t.

The following are equivalent: (i) for every x,t ∈ ℝ there exist qt,qx ∈ ℝ such that τ ↦ q(x,τ) has derivative qt at t, ξ ↦ q(ξ,t) has derivative qx at x, and qt+cqx=0; (ii) p is differentiable over ℝ at every real point.

The following are equivalent: (i) all three conditions hold: for every a,b,t ∈ ℝ the function x ↦ q(x,t) is μ-interval-integrable from a to b; for every x,s,t ∈ ℝ the function τ ↦ c q(x,τ) is μ-interval-integrable from s to t; and for every a,b,s,t ∈ ℝ, ∫_a^b q(x,t) dμ(x) − ∫_a^b q(x,s) dμ(x) = ∫_s^t [c q(a,τ) − c q(b,τ)] dμ(τ); (ii) p is μ-interval-integrable from a to b for every a,b ∈ ℝ.
mathematical_definitions: For real u,v, write (u,v]={r ∈ ℝ : u<r and r≤v}; this set is empty when v≤u.
μ-interval-integrability from a to b means integrability on both (a,b] and (b,a] with respect to μ.
The oriented integral ∫_a^b f(r) dμ(r) means ∫_(a,b] f dμ − ∫_(b,a] f dμ.
Having derivative d at r means ordinary differentiation at r in the full real domain, with derivative value d; no one-sided or restricted-domain derivative is used.
The differential predicate requires separate temporal and spatial derivatives and their equation at every point. It does not itself require joint differentiability or continuous partial derivatives.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every real-valued profile p on the entire real line and every real constant speed c, set q(x,t)=p(x−ct). Five assertions hold together: q agrees with p at time zero; along every line τ ↦ (x+cτ,τ), its value is constantly p(x); the derivative of its restriction to each such line is zero at every time; q has both partial derivatives everywhere satisfying q_t+cq_x=0 exactly when p is differentiable everywhere; and q satisfies spatial interval integrability, temporal interval integrability of the flux cq, and the exact oriented integral balance of spatial content against left flux minus right flux on every rectangle exactly when p is interval integrable on every finite interval. All integration uses the measure μ selected by Real.measureSpace.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: Space, time, profile values and speed are real. Both spatial and temporal domains are all of ℝ, including negative times; there is no bounded domain or boundary condition.
Speed is a fixed constant but may be positive, negative or zero. No nonzero-speed assumption appears.

The first three assertions hold without continuity, measurability, differentiability or integrability assumptions on p. In particular, differentiability of the characteristic restriction does not assert existence of the two partial derivatives.
Even when c=0, the differential predicate still requires the spatial derivative to exist; its multiplication by zero does not remove that requirement.
Even when c=0 and all flux terms vanish, the integral predicate still requires spatial interval integrability of q, and therefore of p.

Neither equivalence asserts that an arbitrary profile actually is differentiable or interval integrable. When the corresponding profile property fails, the associated local predicate is asserted to fail as well.

No endpoint inequalities are assumed. Reversed intervals use oriented integrals. Equal endpoints give empty half-open intervals and trivial individual integral identities, but the universal quantification over all endpoints prevents these cases from making the entire condition vacuous.
The integral predicate includes explicit integrability conditions, so it is not merely an equality between totalized integral expressions for potentially nonintegrable functions.
The profile condition concerns every finite interval; it does not require integrability over the entire real line, finite total mass, boundedness or decay.

The target concerns the explicitly defined q only. It does not quantify over competing solutions or assert uniqueness, a representation theorem for all solutions, entropy admissibility, or a test-function formulation of a weak equation.
The differential predicate does not require continuity of the derivative witnesses as functions of (x,t), and it does not assert C¹ regularity.
All characteristic and initial-value identities are pointwise. The integral balance is an exact equality for every choice of endpoints, not an almost-everywhere assertion about endpoints.
ambiguities: D056 gives Real.measureSpace only as inferInstance. Consequently, the packet fixes a measure μ symbolically but does not expose its construction or normalization sufficiently to verify from the supplied body alone that it is standard Lebesgue measure. The translation retains μ explicitly; if that instance is the usual real volume measure, the integrability condition is ordinary local Lebesgue integrability.
